clinicalPearls: A prominence of the posterosuperior calcaneus rather than an osteonecrosis or traction apophysitis
Affected bone is the calcaneus, specifically its posterosuperior tuberosity behind the Achilles insertion
Typically presents in adults, more often women, and is frequently related to rigid, tight-heeled footwear, hence the term pump bump
Presents with a firm, tender posterolateral heel bump and pain aggravated by shoe wear, often accompanied by retrocalcaneal bursitis and insertional Achilles tendinopathy
The radiographic hallmark is a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity, assessed with lines and angles such as the parallel pitch lines and the Fowler-Philip angle
The combination of the bony prominence, an inflamed retrocalcaneal bursa and Achilles tendinopathy is often termed Haglund syndrome
Local friction between the prominence, the bursa and the Achilles tendon drives the symptoms
Management ranges from footwear modification, heel lifts or orthoses and physiotherapy to surgical resection of the prominence for refractory cases as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Haglund deformity is an enlargement of the posterosuperior prominence of the calcaneal tuberosity that predisposes to mechanical irritation at the back of the heel. The prominent bone lies immediately deep to the retrocalcaneal bursa and adjacent to the insertion of the Achilles tendon. During walking, and particularly when a rigid heel counter compresses the area, the prominence rubs against the bursa and the tendon, producing repetitive friction. This provokes retrocalcaneal bursitis and insertional Achilles tendinopathy, so that the pain of Haglund syndrome arises from the soft-tissue inflammation and tendon degeneration around the bony prominence rather than from the bone itself. A high-arched (cavus) foot posture and a tight Achilles-gastrocnemius complex can accentuate the contact and aggravate symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Sever disease (calcaneal apophysitis) in a skeletally immature patient
Posterior ankle impingement or an os trigonum
Achilles tendon partial tear or ossification
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing lateral heel radiographs to assess the posterosuperior calcaneal prominence
Measurement of parameters such as the parallel pitch lines and Fowler-Philip angle
Ultrasound to evaluate the retrocalcaneal bursa and Achilles insertion
Magnetic resonance imaging to assess insertional tendinopathy, bursitis and bone oedema
Assessment of hindfoot alignment and gastrocnemius-soleus tightness
Footwear assessment to identify a rigid heel counter as a contributing factor
redFlags: Features suggesting an Achilles tendon tear such as a palpable gap or marked weakness of plantarflexion
Rest pain, night pain or systemic features raising concern for infection or tumour
In an adolescent, posterior heel pain more consistent with calcaneal apophysitis than Haglund deformity
Rapidly progressive swelling or erythema suggesting an inflammatory or infective process
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve with footwear modification, offloading and rehabilitation directed at the associated bursitis and Achilles tendinopathy; symptoms can be persistent when conservative measures fail, and surgical resection of the prominence, often with attention to the Achilles insertion, is generally effective in refractory cases.
pitfalls: Attributing all posterior heel pain to the bony prominence and overlooking the associated bursitis and insertional tendinopathy
Injecting the region indiscriminately with corticosteroid and risking Achilles tendon weakening or rupture
Failing to address footwear and a tight gastrocnemius-soleus complex that perpetuate the friction
Confusing the adult deformity with calcaneal apophysitis in a skeletally immature patient
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Footwear modification to remove pressure from a rigid heel counter, using open-backed or soft-heeled shoes and heel lifts
Physiotherapy with gastrocnemius-soleus stretching and eccentric Achilles loading to address the associated insertional tendinopathy
Activity modification, ice and a short course of NSAIDs for painful retrocalcaneal bursitis
Orthoses to correct hindfoot alignment and offload the posterosuperior prominence
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for persistent insertional tendinopathy
Avoid corticosteroid injection into the Achilles insertion given the risk of tendon rupture
Surgical resection of the posterosuperior calcaneal prominence, with Achilles debridement and reattachment as needed, for symptoms refractory to conservative care
